comparator.name: Mathematics
comparator.sourceNotes: The adopted 2026–2027 regulations, current Study Guide and linked timetable establish a 180 EC full-time route. The Algebra and Geometry study path is one set of recommended choices. Year one has 60 EC of required courses. Year two has 30 EC of required courses, 6 EC in Elements of Geometry as the period-six choice and 24 EC of mathematics choices. Year three has 30 EC of open study, 12 EC of mathematics choices, two 3 EC courses and a 12 EC Bachelor Project. The project requires 120 EC after December results and comprises a supervised mathematical investigation, English thesis and oral presentation. The assessment weights are 50% thesis, 30% performance and 20% presentation; the thesis must earn at least 5.5. Passing Study and Career is required for Elements of Geometry credits. The English diagnostic adds no credits. The older recruitment-page reference to Project Mathematics is superseded by the current regulations.

routeSelection.basis: The normalized target is the generic Mathematics bachelor. The 2026-2027 TER defines no formal specialisations, but the year-2 and year-3 constrained choices must be instantiated, and the official 2026-2027 study guide organises them into seven named, non-binding study paths that each satisfy the programme rules; one path is therefore used as a coherent valid pathway. The four interdisciplinary paths (Biomedical Mathematics, Computer Science, Data Science, Optimisation and Economics) add knowledge of another discipline - the TER learning outcome on another discipline applies only to students who follow them - and are more specialised than the three mathematics paths. Algebra and Geometry, Analysis and Dynamical Systems, and Probability and Statistics are equally general: the TER learning outcomes name algebra, geometry, analysis, dynamical systems, probability and statistics together as the main disciplines of mathematics, and none of the three is presented as the default. No path is clearly more representative, so the neutral tie-break selects Algebra and Geometry, the first path in the official order. The choice was fixed before UCR course selection and does not depend on UCR fit. The full-time pace is used; part-time delivery has the same academic curriculum.

core: Calculus and differential-equation techniques, with proof-based analysis explicitly beyond the documented UCR sequence
Linear algebra; abstract group, ring and field theory remains a distinct gap
Discrete mathematics, logic and mathematical reasoning
Probability, statistical inference and stochastic modelling; mathematical-statistics theory and stochastic-system research remain limited
Differential equations, linear systems and Fourier methods; nonlinear dynamical theory and PDE progression remain gaps
Mathematical modelling of real systems and solving real-world problems with mathematics
Programming, numerical methods and mathematical software
History, philosophy and ethics of science and mathematics
Algebra and Geometry study path: rings and fields, Galois theory, geometry, topology and differential topology
Independent bachelor research project in mathematics
questions: How do predator and prey populations change over time, and how can the spread of infectious diseases be modelled and prevented?
How can mathematics improve concrete planning and analysis problems such as hospital operating-room schedules, food-delivery routes, waiting lists and the analysis of satellite images?
How does mathematics contribute to the development of artificial intelligence?

trace: teaches structured and object-oriented programming in Python together with elements of discrete mathematics and computational problem solving, the Python programming skill that VU teaches in its first-year programming course

Teaches differentiation, integration, complex numbers and ordinary differential-equation techniques with quantitative projects. This directly supports the calculus foundation; it does not establish rigorous real analysis or a proof-writing sequence.

Introduces logic, discrete structures and patterns for mathematical decision-making and algorithm construction. The documented profile does not establish the full graph-theory, combinatorics or proof-assessment sequence of VU Discrete Mathematics.

Develops vector spaces, linear transformations, matrices, determinants and eigenvalues, including applications to Fourier series, difference equations and Markov chains. This is substantive mathematical theory and computation, not abstract group/ring/field theory.
Extends calculus to several variables and differential equations using computer algebra. The profile does not establish VU differential forms, general Stokes theorem or proof-based analysis.

develops numerical root finding, interpolation, numerical differentiation and integration and the numerical solution of ordinary differential equations, with explicit attention to accuracy, stability and sensitivity to input

Studies linear time-invariant systems, convolution, Fourier series and transforms, Laplace and Z-transforms. It supplies genuine transform mathematics, without establishing VU Fourier convergence proofs or nonlinear bifurcation/manifold theory.
provides a foundation in mathematical statistics: probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation
introduces research design and descriptive and inferential statistics up to analysis of variance, the applied statistical inference that complements mathematical probability and estimation

develops multivariate statistical models, including linear and logistic regression, factor analysis, analysis of covariance and non-parametric tests, extending statistical inference to models with many variables
teaches the design and performance analysis of algorithms and data structures, applying discrete mathematics and mathematical reasoning about efficiency to computational problems

studies modern algebraic algorithms, fast and arbitrary-precision arithmetic and advanced optimisation methods, giving computational contact with algebraic structures; it complements but does not replace courses in abstract algebra

Teaches discrete/continuous search and constraint satisfaction, with projects in convex optimisation and linear/nonlinear programming. These are substantive computational mathematical methods, without claiming the named hospital or delivery-route examples are taught.

Studies AI planning with uncertainty, partial observability and resource constraints. It applies formal decision techniques, but is not a course in stochastic-process models or VU dynamical-systems theory.
Provides ecological subject knowledge and two weeks of ecological modelling. It is a bounded complementary application setting, not a full mathematical-modelling or dynamical-systems course.

Develops critical appraisal of evidence about disease, risk and population change. This is a complementary empirical setting; the actual profile does not document mathematical epidemic models or optimisation.
Introduces planetary boundaries and sustainability as the subject context and formal gateway for Earth-system tools or Earth Observation. It is not advanced mathematical dynamics.
Uses Earth-system modelling, proxies and isotope tracers to investigate climate. This is a documented modelling application, not a substitute for abstract dynamical-systems or PDE theory.

examines the nature of knowledge and the theoretical methods philosophers use to support conclusions, including the relation of philosophy to physics and computer science, the philosophical reflection on scientific knowledge that the core's philosophy component addresses
develops the main ethical theories and applies them to practical questions, the ethics component of the core

Studies robotic kinematics and motion planning in configuration space, applying geometric and computational reasoning. This is an application of mathematics; it does not supply the group-theoretic, projective/hyperbolic or topological course sequence.

Teaches mathematical/computational image operations including filters, Hough transform and segmentation. It applies computation to images without claiming the specific fluorescence example or proving VU Fourier theory.

Develops regression, classification, resampling, shrinkage, tree methods, support-vector machines and clustering. This is a substantial statistical-learning contribution; it is not the full mathematical theory of statistical estimators.
develops data cleaning, manipulation and visualisation for tabular, spatial and text data in code and ends with an independent data-analysis project answering a research question

Builds and trains neural networks from scratch and with TensorFlow for tabular, image and text data. The actual profile supports theory and implementation; it does not guarantee a particular gradient-proof syllabus.
introduces relational database theory, SQL, normalisation and query processing, the data-management layer of data science

teaches OLS, GLS and instrumental-variables estimation, t, F and LM tests and Monte Carlo study of sampling distributions, applying statistical estimation and testing to data and requiring an empirical paper
treats reinforcement-learning frameworks and algorithms and has students implement agents that learn optimal behaviour from sequential trial-and-error data

Uses GIS to integrate and analyse satellite/drone data on Earth-system change. It is a complementary geospatial application, without claiming the particular fluorescence problem or a mathematical remote-sensing degree.
introduces supply and demand, game theory, consumer and firm theory and market structure, the economic theory on which mathematical economics builds

develops advanced microeconomic theory: decisions under uncertainty, imperfect competition and strategic behaviour, general equilibrium and market efficiency, the subject matter that mathematical economics formalises
analyses market failure, public goods, externalities and taxation with theoretical models and empirical evidence, applying welfare economics to the choice of optimal policy
analyses national income, growth, inflation, unemployment, business cycles and fiscal and monetary policy, the economy-wide dynamics to which economic models are applied

Teaches accounting theory and analysis of financial statements as a business-information complement to economic applications. Its actual profile does not establish capital budgeting, asset pricing, financial mathematics or corporate-finance theory.

alternatives.label: Applied mathematics, modeling and computation
alternatives.labelReason: Numerical methods and algorithms support modeling in robotics, ecology and Earth science.
alternatives.concept: Build a foundation in calculus, linear algebra, discrete mathematics and probability. Use numerical methods, linear systems and algorithms to model problems in robotics, ecology and Earth science.
progression: All72 placements across the three programmes were independently checked against the actual workbook prerequisite and term columns. In this programme, programming precedes algorithmic work; Mathematical Methods precedes every later DISMATH course and courses requiring it; Research Methods and Statistics precedes the economics courses. Linear Algebra and Probability precede Machine Learning where included, and Algorithms precedes Advanced Algorithms. The data alternative places multivariate Statistics in the same term as Machine Learning, after introductory statistics and probability: no extra hard prerequisite is invented. Reinforcement Learning follows Neural Networks in the data alternative, and follows programming/decision/optimisation work in the economics alternative; its actual prerequisite is programming only. Advanced Calculus is in the final spring because the earlier spring courses have restricted offerings. This is feasible under the workbook, though it supplies no VU proof-based progression.

alternatives.label: Mathematical foundations and data science
alternatives.labelReason: Probability, inference and computation support machine learning and data applications.
alternatives.concept: Build a foundation in calculus, linear algebra, discrete mathematics and probability. Apply statistical inference and econometric estimation to data, then explore machine learning, neural networks and decision-making under uncertainty. Use images and geospatial data as applications.
progression: Introductory programming and mathematical methods precede the advanced mathematics and computing courses. Data Science precedes Computer Vision and Machine Learning. Machine Learning precedes Neural Networks & Deep Learning. Research Methods & Statistics precedes Econometrics.
alternatives.distinctness: This option emphasizes data management, image and geospatial data, statistical inference and neural networks. The modeling option emphasizes robotics, numerical applications in natural systems and optimization.
traceOverrides: Develops regression, classification, resampling, shrinkage, tree methods, support-vector machines and clustering. This is a substantial statistical-learning contribution; it is not the full mathematical theory of statistical estimators.

Teaches mathematical/computational image operations including filters, Hough transform and segmentation. It applies computation to images without claiming the specific fluorescence example or proving VU Fourier theory.

Develops critical appraisal of evidence about disease, risk and population change. This is a complementary empirical setting; the actual profile does not document mathematical epidemic models or optimisation.
Introduces planetary boundaries and sustainability as the subject context and formal gateway for Earth-system tools or Earth Observation. It is not advanced mathematical dynamics.

alternatives.label: Mathematical methods, optimization and economics
alternatives.labelReason: Mathematical methods support algorithmic optimization, economic inquiry and econometrics.
alternatives.concept: Build a foundation in calculus, linear algebra, probability and numerical methods. Use algorithms and AI to study optimization and decision-making. Apply quantitative methods to economic behavior, public policy and econometric estimation.
progression: All72 placements across the three programmes were independently checked against the actual workbook prerequisite and term columns. In this programme, programming precedes algorithmic work; Mathematical Methods precedes every later DISMATH course and courses requiring it; Research Methods and Statistics precedes the economics courses. Linear Algebra and Probability precede Machine Learning where included, and Algorithms precedes Advanced Algorithms. The data alternative places multivariate Statistics in the same term as Machine Learning, after introductory statistics and probability: no extra hard prerequisite is invented. Reinforcement Learning follows Neural Networks in the data alternative, and follows programming/decision/optimisation work in the economics alternative; its actual prerequisite is programming only. Advanced Calculus is in the final spring because the earlier spring courses have restricted offerings. This is feasible under the workbook, though it supplies no VU proof-based progression.
alternatives.distinctness: This option emphasizes microeconomics, macroeconomics and public policy, paired with econometrics, optimization and advanced algorithms. Its economic sequence differs from both natural-system modeling and computational data analysis.
traceOverrides: Teaches discrete/continuous search and constraint satisfaction, with projects in convex optimisation and linear/nonlinear programming. These are substantive computational mathematical methods, without claiming the named hospital or delivery-route examples are taught.

Studies AI planning with uncertainty, partial observability and resource constraints. It applies formal decision techniques, but is not a course in stochastic-process models or VU dynamical-systems theory.
studies modern algebraic algorithms and advanced solution methods for optimisation problems with emphasis on mathematical modelling, extending optimisation into algorithm design
treats reinforcement-learning frameworks and algorithms for learning optimal policies in sequential decision problems, a computational approach to dynamic optimisation under uncertainty
teaches OLS, GLS and instrumental-variables estimation and t, F and LM tests with Monte Carlo analysis and requires an empirical paper, the statistical estimation of economic relationships

candidates.label: Proof-based pure mathematics
candidates.assessment: UCR offers genuine calculus, vector-space theory, probability and Fourier/algorithmic methods, but no documented sustained proof-writing, rigorous real/complex analysis, abstract algebra, geometry/topology or nonlinear theoretical sequence. Applied methods cannot own these pure-mathematics interests. This limitation is explicit in every retained alternative.

selection.assessment: Three options share seven mathematical courses and differ by 6, 7 and 8 courses per side across the three pairs. The choices support distinct sequences in modeling, statistical data analysis and optimization with economics. UCR does not sustain a separate pure-mathematics sequence in proof-based analysis, abstract algebra and geometry. Computer science and biomedical applications were considered. The three retained options have stronger coherent mathematics applications; a mathematics-teaching option lacks specialist pedagogy.

blocks: Both teach differentiation, integration, complex numbers and differential-equation techniques. The VU outline also specifies convergence of series, Taylor series and simple epsilon proofs; those are not established by the UCR profile. This is a qualified subject relationship.

Both treat calculus of several variables. VU explicitly includes differential forms and general Stokes theorem; the UCR profile establishes multivariable calculus/differential equations but not that complete vector-calculus syllabus.

Both develop discrete mathematical reasoning. VU specifies graph theory, combinatorics, flows, generating functions and proofs. The UCR profile supports logic/discrete structures and algorithmic applications, without establishing every listed VU topic.
VU introduces mathematical argument and proof in a dedicated course. UCR develops some of these techniques in Logic & Discrete Mathematics.
VU develops rigorous proofs about calculus and continuity. UCR emphasizes methods and applications.

Complex Analysis studies functions of a complex variable. Advanced Calculus touches complex-valued functions but is a calculus course already matched to Multivariable Calculus; UCR has no complex-analysis course.
VU studies partial differential equations in a dedicated course. UCR’s calculus and numerical courses include ordinary differential equations.

Both study vector spaces, matrices, linear transformations, determinants and eigenvalues. VU also explicitly assesses small proofs, QR/SVD and inner-product methods; the UCR profile does not establish that full assessment/syllabus.
Group Theory is the first abstract-algebra course. UCR has no abstract-algebra course; Advanced Algorithms treats algebraic algorithms computationally and is not claimed as a counterpart.
Rings and Fields continues abstract algebra. UCR has no counterpart.
VU advances its abstract algebra sequence through field extensions and Galois theory.

Elements of Geometry is a geometry course taken as a practical exercise. UCR has no geometry course; Robotics uses geometric reasoning about configuration spaces for motion planning but is not a geometry course, so no counterpart is claimed.
Topology studies topological spaces and continuity abstractly. UCR has no counterpart.
Differential Topology is an advanced course on smooth manifolds. UCR has no counterpart.
Dynamical systems, Fourier analysis & modelling of real systems

Both study Fourier series and Fourier transforms. UCR approaches them through linear time-invariant systems and convolution, adding Laplace/Z-transforms; VU develops convergence, summability, Plancherel theory, proofs and PDE applications. This is partial mathematical correspondence.

Dynamical Systems is the core course on the mathematical theory of systems evolving in time. Linear Systems treats only linear time-invariant systems and is already matched to Fourier Analysis, and no other UCR course develops dynamical-systems theory, so no counterpart is claimed.

Mathematical Modelling of Dynamical Systems translates real systems, such as predator-prey populations, into dynamical models. Ecosystems Uncovered spends two weeks on ecological modelling and Earth System Science Tools teaches Earth-system modelling, but both are science courses in which modelling is one component rather than the mathematical subject itself, so neither is claimed as a counterpart.

Both teach mathematical probability and discrete/continuous distributions. VU details joint/conditional distributions and the central limit theorem; UCR additionally includes estimation and simulation, without documentation of every VU theoretical topic.

VU develops frequentist and Bayesian estimators, tests, confidence sets and their mathematical comparison. UCR’s probability course is already paired to Probability Theory; applied Research Methods and Statistics does not establish this mathematical-statistics course. No separate counterpart is claimed.

Mathematical Modelling of Stochastic Systems models random processes evolving in time. Decision-making in AI concerns planning under uncertainty rather than stochastic-process modelling, and Linear Algebra treats Markov chains only as an application, so no counterpart is claimed.
Both teach programming in Python from scratch. UCR's course is a full course that also covers object-oriented programming and elements of discrete mathematics; VU's is a 3-EC introduction.

Both teach numerical root finding, interpolation, numerical integration and ODE solution with accuracy/reliability. VU additionally specifies Matlab, eigenvalue/least-squares problems, FFT and PDE applications; these are not all established in the UCR profile.

Introduction to Mathematical Modelling, LaTeX and Mathematica teaches mathematical software and typesetting for modelling work. UCR mathematics courses use computer algebra software within their content, but no UCR course is dedicated to mathematical software and typesetting.

Both address ethics as part of the programme. Philosophy and Ethics is a 3-EC course for science students; UCR's Ethics is a full course in moral theory and practical ethics and shares its ethical component, not any philosophy-of-science content.
History of Science is a 3-EC course on the historical development of science. No UCR course in these alternatives treats the history of science, so no counterpart is claimed.
Personal development, open profiling space & research
VU reserves 30 EC for approved open study.
VU requires a 12 EC individual mathematics project and thesis. UCR’s optional independent research is outside the scheduled 180 EC.

notes.text: The UCR options develop mathematical methods and their applications. VU devotes more coursework to formal proof, real and complex analysis, abstract algebra and topology. VU requires an individual mathematics thesis. UCR’s optional independent research is outside the scheduled 180 EC.

audience.programmeDescription: VU Mathematics combines mathematical proof and abstraction with calculus, algebra, geometry, analysis, probability, statistics and modelling. Students develop theoretical reasoning and computational skills, choose a flexible study pathway and complete an individual mathematics research project.
audience.comparisonExplanation: All three UCR options develop calculus, linear algebra, probability and numerical methods, then apply them to modeling, data science or optimization and economics. VU has a deeper sequence in proof-based analysis, abstract algebra, geometry and topology, and requires an individual mathematics project.
